opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that OpenClaw feels closer to what an agent should be than a product built around a fixed workflow. Many agent products today are really carefully designed pipelines: someone has decided in advance which steps the model takes, which tools it calls, and in what order. That works for demos and narrow use cases, but you quickly hit a ceiling. OpenClaw gives the model much more freedom. It lives in your real environment, with your files, your terminal, your messaging apps, and it decides for itself how to get things done. As someone who trains models, that is exactly what I want to see, because it shows what the model can actually do rather than what the framework designer anticipated.

The second reason is that it's open and fast-moving. I always use the latest version because the community iterates so quickly. New skills, new integrations, better memory handling appear almost every week. With a closed product you wait for the company's roadmap. Here, if something is missing, someone has often already built it, or you can build it yourself in an afternoon. That openness matters a lot to me, partly because I come from the open-source model world, and I believe the ecosystem improves fastest when everyone can see and change everything.

The third reason is more personal. Using it every day is the best way to understand where models still fall short. When I give it a real task, like organizing research notes, following up on experiments, or handling a messy multi-step job, I see exactly where it gets confused, loses context, or overestimates itself. That feedback is incredibly valuable for thinking about the next generation of models. A polished product hides the failures. OpenClaw shows them to you directly, and for a researcher, that honesty is worth more than smoothness.

Of course, it's not perfect. It can be rough, it requires some setup, and you have to think carefully about permissions and security, because you're handing a lot of control to an agent. But to me, that roughness is part of the point. It feels like the early days of something important, and I'd rather be using the thing at the frontier than a safer version that's already a step behind.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenClaw’s community iterates quickly, but does not state that Fuli Luo has never seen another agent framework or product advance faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first reason is a bit personal: I wanted an agent I could actually live inside of, not one I had to visit. Most agent products I tried were still essentially chat windows with tools bolted on. You open an app, you type, something happens, you close it. OpenClaw flipped that. It sits in the channels I already use, it runs on a machine I control, and it stays around between conversations. That changes how you relate to it. It stops being a demo and starts being a colleague who remembers what we were doing yesterday.

The second reason is the openness. I have spent a lot of years around models and training pipelines, so I am allergic to black boxes. With OpenClaw I can read the loop, see how memory is stored, see what context gets assembled before each call, and swap the model underneath when I want to. If something goes wrong I can trace it. That matters a lot when you want to use an agent for real work rather than a weekend experiment.

The third thing is the community. The skills ecosystem grew very fast, and that is not an accident. The abstraction is simple enough that ordinary developers can write something useful in an afternoon, but it is not so simple that it becomes a toy. A lot of frameworks pick one side of that trade-off. OpenClaw found a reasonable middle.

I will be fair and say it is not perfect. Security and permissions are still something you have to think about carefully yourself, and the setup is not for someone who has never touched a terminal. But for me, as someone who wants to push on what agents can do and also understand why they do it, that trade is worth it. The latest versions in particular feel like the moment when the framework stopped chasing features and started refining the core loop, and that is usually the sign that a tool is maturing.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenClaw’s skills ecosystem grew very fast, but does not state that no other agent framework or product has advanced faster.

astra-6.text:
For me, the main criterion is how much friction there is between having an idea and getting an agent to carry it out. I care about being able to experiment, understand what went wrong, and adjust the workflow without fighting the framework.

That’s the lens through which I’d explain my preference for the latest OpenClaw. It’s not that one framework is universally better. I’m looking for a good balance between something useful out of the box and something I can still control and extend. The newest version matters only if it improves that experience—not simply because it’s new.

r001.rationale: The response describes low friction, flexibility, and the value of OpenClaw’s latest version, but does not say its open-source community advances faster than any other framework or product.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the key is how well an agent fits into the way I actually work. I want to give it a goal, let it carry out the steps, and still be able to understand what it’s doing and steer it when needed. That’s the balance I look for in OpenClaw: useful autonomy with enough control. I wouldn’t say it’s universally better than every other framework; it’s about which one creates the least friction for the tasks I care about.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses OpenClaw’s fit, autonomy, and control, but does not say its open-source community has advanced faster than any other agent framework or product.
